forces: Flute, solo violin, obbligato harpsichord, strings and continuo
performers: Advent Chamber Orchestra; Roxana Pavel Goldstein, violin; Constance Schoepflin, flute; Matthew Ganong, harpsichord
intro: Flute, violin and harpsichord share the solo passages until the keyboard takes the room to itself. Bach writes out sixty-five bars of unaccompanied harpsichord: the instrument that usually supports everyone else becomes the whole concerto.

sections.label: A · Strings in D major
sections.mNote: The violins share the opening refrain; the flute waits

sections.label: C · Soloists in minor keys
sections.mNote: Keyboard runs thread between the string refrains

sections.label: D · The D-major string refrain
sections.mNote: The violins recover the home key

sections.label: E · Flute and violin over keyboard
sections.mNote: The solo lines continue above the harpsichord’s running notes

sections.label: F · Keyboard runs and string refrains
sections.mNote: The harpsichord’s solo writing grows longer

sections.label: Cadenza · Harpsichord alone
sections.mNote: Two hands supply every part for sixty-five bars

sections.label: A · The strings return
sections.mNote: The opening D-major refrain closes the movement

relations.label: The opening ritornello returns
relations.basis: The opening and final ritornellos frame the solo episodes and written-out cadenza; the section map places the final tutti near 568 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.954, sustained 17 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 566.5 s (cache/form/bach-brandenburg-5-allegro.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: The flute waits
cues.text: The two violin parts play the same brisk D-major refrain over a moving bass. The flute is silent. This refrain is the ritornello, the music the strings bring back between the soloists’ excursions.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft full score (1871), I, opening eight bars. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ed/IMSLP02043-BWV1050.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Three soloists at work
cues.text: Flute and violin exchange short phrases, with the harpsichord’s right hand joining them. Its left hand still has the bass to play. Bach writes the keyboard’s solo notes out in full, alongside the figured bass used for accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), I, from bar 9; the harpsichord alternates written-out solo passages with figured-bass accompaniment.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A month under arrest
cues.text: In 1717 Bach signs a contract with Prince Leopold at Köthen before securing permission to leave Weimar. His employer refuses his resignation and has him confined for a month. In December he is released and dismissed; he can finally take up the new job.

cues.title: Eighteen bars become sixty-five
cues.text: An earlier version gives the harpsichord an eighteen-bar solo. For the score dedicated to the Margrave of Brandenburg in 1721, Bach expands it to sixty-five. Flute and violin get nothing remotely comparable.
cues.evidence: Comparison of BWV 1050.1 and BWV 1050.2, including the expanded cadenza. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandenburg_Concerto_No._5

cues.title: A harpsichord from Berlin
cues.text: In March 1719 Bach travels from Köthen to Berlin to collect a new harpsichord for Prince Leopold’s court. On that visit he probably plays for Margrave Christian Ludwig: in the 1721 dedication of these concertos Bach recalls doing so “a couple of years ago”.
cues.evidence: Netherlands Bach Society, notes on BWV 1050: Bach’s dedication preface and the March 1719 Berlin visit to receive a new harpsichord for Köthen. https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-1050

cues.title: Concerts at the coffeehouse
cues.text: From 1729 Bach directs Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum, whose weekly concerts at Café Zimmermann move outdoors in summer. The programmes include his orchestral suites and his violin and harpsichord concertos, and give him a platform as a keyboard player.

cues.title: The keyboard takes over
cues.text: Everyone else stops. The harpsichord keeps the bass and spins increasingly elaborate figures above it. This enormous solo is written into the score, down to its fastest notes; the orchestra waits through sixty-five bars.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), I, bars 154–218. The formal boundaries are tabulated by San Francisco Conservatory: https://sfcm.edu/sites/default/files/sfcm-theory/analysis_lectures/21_concerto/brandenburg_5_chart.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two hands, a whole ensemble
cues.text: Bach gives the keyboard the broken chords and rapid alternations that a concerto might save for a virtuoso violinist. The left hand keeps supplying bass notes while the right ranges above it. The unaccompanied solo has its own accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), I, extended cadenza; the transfer of violin techniques to the keyboard is discussed at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandenburg_Concerto_No._5.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: The strings come back
cues.text: The strings recover their D-major refrain. After the long keyboard solo, the familiar violin unison sounds wonderfully plain. The harpsichord returns to accompanying, and the flute sits out the close just as it sat out the opening.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), I, bar 219 to the end, p. 148: string ritornello, flute rests and harpsichord marked accomp.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The flute joins the conversation
transitions.how: The eight-bar string refrain closes in D major. Flute and solo violin begin exchanging phrases above the harpsichord’s bass, with the keyboard’s right hand joining their runs. The pulse continues; the solo episode carries the music towards A major, where the next string refrain arrives.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), I, bars 1–19; San Francisco Conservatory form chart: https://sfcm.edu/sites/default/files/sfcm-theory/analysis_lectures/21_concerto/brandenburg_5_chart.pdf

transitions.title: The harpsichord keeps the bass
transitions.from: F · Keyboard runs and string refrains
transitions.how: The other players stop, leaving the harpsichord with both bass and upper parts. Its solo prolongs A major, the dominant of D. Sequences, broken chords and ever smaller note values fill the space before the strings can recover their refrain.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), I, bars 154–218; dominant function and cadenza boundaries in the San Francisco Conservatory form chart.

transitions.title: The violins recover D major
transitions.how: The harpsichord’s last running figures lead into the opening violin refrain in D major. The keyboard changes to accompaniment, marked accomp., and the string basses return beneath the violins. The flute remains silent through the closing refrain.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), I, p. 148: end of the cadenza and final ritornello, from bar 219.

source.title: Bach, Brandenburg Concerto No. 5, BWV 1050, full score (Bach-Gesellschaft, 1871)
source.locator: I. Allegro, printed pp. 127–148: flute, solo violin, harpsichord, ripieno violin, viola, cello and violone. The solo keyboard cadenza occupies bars 154–218. The flute rests in the opening and closing string refrains.

timeline.note: Solo and ripieno violins play the opening refrain. The flute rests while the strings and harpsichord supply the bass.
Flute, violin and harpsichord begin their exchanges. The ripieno strings join them for the returning refrains.
Flute and violin trade phrases above the harpsichord’s quick notes and the accompanying strings.
The strings keep returning to their refrain as the harpsichord’s runs grow longer.
The harpsichord plays alone, supplying bass, chords and racing upper lines through the cadenza.
The strings return with the opening refrain. The harpsichord accompanies; the flute remains silent.

composer.epithet: He supplied Leipzig’s churches with music for twenty-seven years and left keyboard players enough work for a lifetime.
facts: His brother Johann Christoph in Ohrdruf; St Michael’s School, Lüneburg
Organist, teacher, cantor and director of Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum
Cantatas and Passions; organ and keyboard collections; concertos and solo string music
composer.background:
Bach grew up in a house full of working musicians. His father, Johann Ambrosius, served the town of Eisenach; apprentices lived with the family, and relatives held church and civic posts across Thuringia. Johann Sebastian was born in 1685. His mother died when he was nine, his father the following year, and he moved to Ohrdruf to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist taught by Pachelbel. He sang in the school choir and learnt the organ at home. At fifteen he went to St Michael’s School in Lüneburg, where his voice helped pay for his education. In 2006 some of his schoolboy copies of north German organ works, including two of the hardest pieces of the day, turned up in the Anna Amalia Library in Weimar.

In 1702 he won the organist’s post at Sangerhausen, until the duke intervened and gave it to someone else. The next year Arnstadt hired him to examine its new organ and then to play it. Two years later he set off on foot to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck. He stayed for months, far beyond his authorised leave, and came back to a reprimand. In 1707 he moved to Mühlhausen and on 17 October married his second cousin Maria Barbara at Dornheim. The cantata for the inauguration of Mühlhausen’s town council in February 1708, Gott ist mein König, BWV 71, was one of the few works printed in his lifetime. His cantata Aus der Tiefen, BWV 131, already makes two people say different things together: one sings the psalmist’s plea, another a hymn in long notes above it.
